title: Kerala Consumer Commission Orders Immigration Firm to Refund ₹75,000 in Visa Fraud Case
excerpt: The state panel upheld a district commission ruling against Amster Immigration Overseas, finding that the consultancy collected fees before signing any agreement and failed to deliver on its promise of Canadian permanent residency services.
body:
• The Kerala State Consumer Commission dismissed an appeal by Amster Immigration Overseas Pvt. Ltd. and upheld a refund order of ₹75,000 with 9% interest, plus ₹25,000 in compensation and ₹15,000 in combined costs.
  • The commission found the consultancy collected fees before executing any agreement and failed to take substantive steps toward securing a Canadian PR visa for the complainant.
  • The ruling adds to a growing body of consumer court decisions cracking down on immigration consultancies that collect large fees without delivering services, including a recent ₹12.35 lakh refund order in Chandigarh.

Commission Finds 'Unjust Enrichment'

The Kerala State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has dismissed an appeal by Amster Immigration Overseas Pvt. Ltd. and affirmed a district commission order directing the firm to refund ₹75,000 with 9% interest, pay ₹25,000 in compensation, and cover ₹5,000 in litigation costs to a woman who sought Canadian permanent residency services.

The state commission went further, imposing an additional ₹10,000 in costs on the consultancy for pursuing the appeal, bringing the total payout to over ₹1.15 lakh.

The case, Amster Immigration Overseas Pvt. Ltd. v. Ruksana Nazlin M. (First Appeal No. 16 of 2024), was decided on January 9, 2026, by a bench comprising Justice B. Sudheendra Kumar (President), Ajith Kumar D. (Judicial Member), and K. R. Radhakrishnan (Member).

How the Fraud Unfolded

The complainant, Ruksana Nazlin, paid ₹76,190 to Amster Immigration on November 30, 2020 — ₹75,000 for processing fees toward a Canadian PR visa and ₹1,190 as an assessment fee. The consultancy had assured her the amount would be refunded if she cancelled the plan.

Two days later, the firm sent an email with a blank preliminary agreement — already signed by its manager — that retrospectively characterised the payment as non-refundable. No main agreement was ever executed or signed by the complainant.

The commission noted this sequence cast "serious doubt" on the consultancy's claim that the fee was contractually non-refundable, given the money was collected before any agreement existed.

According to the complaint, Amster Immigration did little beyond creating an ICES account for Educational Credential Assessment. The application was rejected twice for being incomplete, and the complainant was unable to clear IELTS and ECA owing to financial difficulties during the COVID-19 pandemic. When she sought a refund, the firm refused and suggested arbitration — despite no arbitration agreement existing between the parties.

"No material had been produced to show that any substantive steps were taken by the consultancy towards Permanent Resident documentation, nor was there evidence of any loss suffered by it."

— Kerala State Consumer Commission

A Pattern of Predatory Practices

The Kerala ruling is part of a broader pattern of consumer court interventions against immigration consultancies across India. In a separate case decided this year, a District Consumer Commission in Chandigarh ordered a visa consultant to refund ₹12.35 lakh to a 21-year-old woman after finding that forged admission documents were used to make her believe she had secured admission to a Canadian college. The college, Academy of Learning, confirmed in writing that no admission record existed in her name.

The Ministry of External Affairs has repeatedly warned against unregistered recruitment agents, noting a "huge rise" in overseas job seekers being cheated through fake job offers. Under the Emigration Act of 1983, licensed recruiting agents may not charge more than ₹30,000 plus 18% GST in service fees — a threshold frequently breached by unlicensed operators.

What Prospective Emigrants Should Know

The rulings underscore several precautions for Indians considering overseas employment or immigration. Consumer protection law under Section 2(47) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, defines the failure to refund service charges for undelivered services as a deficiency in service and unfair trade practice. Complaints can be filed before District Consumer Commissions within two years of the cause of action.

The Ministry of External Affairs maintains a public registry of licensed recruiting agents at emigrate.gov.in. Prospective emigrants are advised to verify an agent's licence number, insist on a signed employment contract before making payments, and confirm that the visa type being arranged is an employment or work visa rather than a tourist visa.

For diaspora families funding the immigration journeys of relatives in India, the message from consumer courts is clear: demand written agreements upfront, verify all documentation independently, and pursue formal consumer complaints promptly if services are not delivered.
